summary: This informational RFC describes a use case for congestion exposure, ConEx, in mobile networks that resemble the 3GPP Evolved Packet System. It gives a short overview of the access and core architecture and explains where ConEx information could be used in such networks.

eli5.summary: Cars on a road could show a sign saying how crowded the road is. This looks at how phone networks could use such signs.

subtitle: Use congestion signals to manage traffic and resources in 3GPP mobile networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile networks have scarce resources (spectrum, backhaul capacity) and face unpredictable demand. Today they use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) and static rules to manage traffic, which is complex and inflexible. With encrypted traffic rising, DPI works less well.
tldr.mechanism: Congestion Exposure (ConEx) lets hosts mark packets with their contribution to congestion. The network reads these marks and enforces policies: penalize heavy-traffic flows, offer incentives to light-traffic users, or account for congestion volume like volume-based billing.
tldr.outcome: Mobile networks can manage traffic more dynamically and efficiently without needing to inspect packets or know application types. Both the network and applications get real-time congestion information to respond appropriately.

facts.label: Key function placement
facts.value: Auditing at eNB; Policing at P-GW

facts.label: Traffic composition
facts.value: Most flows are short; few cause majority of volume

facts.label: Deployment scenarios
facts.value: 4 (server ConEx, full end-to-end, isolated domains, ConEx Lite)

today: RFC 7778 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It provides guidance for deploying Congestion Exposure in 3GPP mobile networks, complementing the ConEx protocol specifications (RFCs 6789 and 7713).

sections.title: The Mobile Network Challenge
sections.content:
Mobile networks (3GPP LTE and 5G) provide connectivity to millions of users over shared radio spectrum. The spectrum is expensive and limited. Demand varies by location and time: a stadium during a concert is congested; the same stadium at midnight is empty.

Most traffic is not urgent: OS updates, app downloads, video streaming. A small fraction of users generates most of the traffic. This creates a fairness problem: how do operators share resources fairly when a few heavy users could starve everyone else?

Today, operators use Deep Packet Inspection (DPI): devices scan packet contents to identify the application (video, social media, email) and apply policies accordingly. Gold subscribers get priority; free-tier subscribers get best-effort. But DPI is expensive, complex, and breaks with encrypted traffic.

Congestion Exposure (ConEx) offers an alternative: instead of inspecting packets, let the application itself tell the network how much congestion it caused. The network rewards cooperative apps and penalizes cheaters.
sections.eli5: Today a school assigns playground time by looking at what game each kid is playing. Tomorrow, a kid could say 'I am a heavy player, give someone else the swing,' and the school gives the swing to someone else.

sections.title: How ConEx Works in Mobile
sections.content:
ConEx is a feedback loop. When a sender (phone, server) detects that the network is congested—via ECN (Explicit Congestion Notification) or timeout—it marks outgoing packets with ConEx flags saying 'I contributed to congestion.' Network devices (base stations, gateways) read these marks and enforce policy.

Four use cases stand out for mobile networks:

1. Dynamic Traffic Management. Instead of static, DPI-based classes (video, email, etc.), a policer can make decisions based on real ConEx signals. High-congestion flows can be throttled. Low-congestion flows get priority. This adapts to actual network load, not predictions.

2. Incentivizing Light-Weight Transports. LEDBAT is a transport that backs off quickly when congestion appears, leaving bandwidth for others. Today, apps do not use it because users have no reward. With ConEx-based billing ('users with low congestion contribution pay less'), incentives align.

3. Congestion-Based Billing. Instead of 'you used 10 GB, pay $5,' operators could bill 'you caused 50 units of congestion, pay $5.' Fair users with lightweight apps pay less. Heavy users pay more. This is already technically feasible in 3GPP Policy and Charging Control (PCC) systems.

4. Selective Traffic Offload. When a user has both LTE and Wi-Fi available, decisions about which flows to offload are often static. ConEx could make them dynamic: offload the flows causing most congestion.
sections.eli5: Instead of the teacher assigning games by looking at the game, the kids mark their game with how much recess space they are using. The teacher gives space to the kids using least space.

sections.title: 3GPP Networks and ConEx
sections.content:
A 3GPP mobile network has standardized components: User Equipment (UE, the phone), base stations (eNB), a Serving Gateway (S-GW), and a Packet Data Network Gateway (P-GW). Data flows through tunnels (GTP or PMIPv6) between these components.

ConEx can be deployed in several ways. One scenario: web servers and content caches support ConEx; phones do not. The P-GW (the operator's gateway to the Internet) reads ConEx marks from servers and enforces policy at the network edge, without changing any phones.

Another scenario: everyone is ConEx-enabled. Phones mark packets, servers mark packets, and the network reads both. This gives full visibility into congestion contribution per application per user.

A third scenario ('ConEx Lite'): phones do not mark packets; instead, a tunnel receiver monitors losses and ECN marks inside the tunnel and informs the tunnel sender how much congestion occurred. The sender then learns and adjusts.

The RFC emphasizes: ConEx is optional and partial. An operator can deploy it without waiting for all devices to support it. Non-ConEx users can be treated with fixed volume caps; ConEx users with dynamic policies.
sections.eli5: The network is a mix of smart phones (that understand ConEx) and older phones (that do not). The network can treat them differently: smart phones get flexible limits, older phones get fixed caps.

sections.title: Deployment Strategies and Scenarios
sections.content:
ConEx protocol mechanisms are already defined (IPv6 destination options, TCP modifications). The main step is adding ConEx support to senders: phones, servers, caches. Receivers do not need to change initially.

For 3GPP networks, ConEx functions should be placed carefully. An auditing function (checking if apps are cheating about congestion) should go at the end of the path—typically the base station (eNB)—where it can see actual losses and ECN marks.

A policing function (enforcing policy) should be co-located with the P-GW, which already connects to the Policy and Charging Rule Function (PCRF) for per-user policies and quotas. This allows operators to enforce per-subscriber limits.

Important consideration: mobile networks extensively use tunneling (GTP, PMIPv6). ConEx information must be copied from the inner header (where applications set it) to the outer tunnel header (where the network reads it). This requires specific tunneling behavior, similar to ECN handling defined in RFC 6040.

Mobility is another consideration. When a phone moves between base stations during a call, the network must track congestion contribution across the handover. This is complex but feasible with distributed rate limiting techniques already studied in research.

Real-World Scenarios. A server-side deployment: Netflix, YouTube, and weather apps on servers mark their ConEx signals. The P-GW reads marks and throttles flows causing high congestion. Non-ConEx apps get throttled only when other mechanisms kick in. ConEx apps can optimize their bit rate and get better throughput.

An end-to-end deployment: all phones, servers, and operators support ConEx. A phone doing a video call marks packets with low ConEx (careful, real-time protocol). A phone doing a background update marks packets with high ConEx (can tolerate delay). The network sees both and assigns bandwidth accordingly.

A congestion-based billing scenario: the operator uses the PCC architecture (already in 3GPP) to bill by congestion units instead of bytes. A user who streams video using LEDBAT (which detects congestion and backs off) racks up fewer congestion units than a user streaming the same video with a greedy transport. Both use 10 GB; the LEDBAT user pays less.

ConEx works incrementally: deploy on servers first, then phones, then operators. Each step adds value without requiring the others.
sections.eli5: Put an audit clerk at the radio tower (to check if apps are lying), and a policy clerk at the gateway (to apply rules per subscriber). A helpful app (like one using LEDBAT) tells the network 'I am backing off for you,' and the network rewards it. A greedy app does not back off, and pays more.

sections.title: Security and Auditing
sections.content:
A key risk: apps might lie. A malicious or buggy app could claim 'I caused no congestion' even while sending at maximum rate. Or claim 'I caused huge congestion' to waste operator resources.

ConEx includes an auditing function to catch this. Auditing is done by comparing what the app claims (via ConEx marks) against what actually happened (via ECN, packet loss, queue length). If claims do not match reality, the flow is penalized.

Auditing can be per-flow (inspect every packet) or aggregate (sample flows). Mobile networks with expensive resources might favor aggregate auditing for efficiency, accepting some uncertainty.

The RFC references RFC 7713, which details ConEx security. The key point: ConEx is not foolproof, but it is better than no feedback. Even if some apps cheat, most cooperating apps still benefit the network.
sections.eli5: If an app lies and says 'I caused no congestion' when it really did, the network's auditor catches it by checking reality. Once caught, the app is penalized.

sections.title: ConEx as a Network Solution
sections.content:
ConEx is not a replacement for QoS. It is a supplement that makes QoS simpler and more dynamic. Instead of the network guessing application intent (DPI), applications expose their congestion contribution, and the network responds based on actual data.

The RFC identifies key requirements for ConEx in mobile networks:

  • Performance: Mobile networks have high loss and delay. ConEx signals must reflect real conditions, not stale information.
  • Mobility: When a phone moves, congestion state follows. The ConEx scheme must track per-user state across handovers.
  • Multi-Access: Phones with dual LTE and Wi-Fi need ConEx signals for both paths so the network can decide which to use.
  • Tunneling: ConEx information must work with GTP and PMIPv6 tunnels, carrying signals from inner to outer headers as needed.
  • Roaming: When a user roams into a different operator, ConEx policies may differ. The network must handle this gracefully.

The RFC concludes that ConEx is quite feasible for 3GPP networks as a per-operator-domain deployment, without waiting for global standardization. Operators can start small and grow.
sections.eli5: ConEx is an idea that lets mobile networks understand congestion without spying on apps. It works best when the network is honest and audits claims, and apps are cooperative and truthful.
